## Recap

-   We have seen how to perform hypothesis tests for questions involving the following:

    -   A single proportion (Middle "berry" vs "burry")

    -   Independence of two categorical variables (banker sex discrimination)

        -   Think of as one population

    -   Difference in two proportions (blood thinner)

        -   Think of as two populations

-   We are now going to see another hypothesis test, this time for *numerical* data

# Test for a single mean

## Running example + form hypotheses

We will use the the data I collected from you about average hours of sleep per night.

::: discuss
What type of variable(s) do we have?
:::

-   I know most college students don't receive the recommended 8 hours of sleep. But what about 7.5 hours?

```{r echo = F}
mu0 <- 7.5
```

-   Before we look at the data, we should form our hypotheses. Suppose I am interested in learning if Middlebury students who have an 8:15am class get at most 7.5 hours of sleep (on average).

-   ::: discuss
    What might our hypotheses be?
    :::

    -   $H_{0}$: $\mu =$ `r mu0` versus $H_{A}$: $\mu <$ `r mu0`, where $\mu$ is the true mean of the average hours of sleep Middlebury students with an 8:15 am class get.
        -   Terminology: I will refer to $\mu_{0} =$ `r mu0` as my "null hypothesized value". (i.e. the specific value of $\mu$ in $H_{0}$)

## Collect and summarise data

```{r}
dat <- read_csv("../data/stat201_data.csv")
sleep <- dat$avg_sleep
n <- length(sleep)
xbar <- round(mean(sleep), 3)
```

```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = avg_sleep)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Average sleep per night (hours)") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 24))
```

The observed/sample mean of average hours of sleep per night is $\bar{x}_{obs} =$ `r xbar` from a sample of `r n` students

-   Now we must determine if we have "convincing evidence"! Choose $\alpha = 0.05$

## Simulating null distribution

To simulate from the null distribution, we need to operate in a world where $H_{0}$ is true.

-   So, I need to repeatedly simulate data sets of size `r n` where true mean is $\mu_{0} =$ `r mu0`, without changing anything else

    -   Specifically, my hypotheses aren't saying anything about spread, just center!

-   If I don't want to make any assumptions about how the data behave, how might I do that?

## Recap bootstrap (NOT exactly the strategy)

::: discuss
How would I obtain a bootstrap distribution of the sample mean of mean hours of sleep?
:::

:::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="30%"}
:::: fragment
::: discuss
Remind ourselves: Where should the bootstrap distribution be centered?
:::
::::
:::::

:::: {.column width="70%"}
::: fragment
```{r}
B <- 5000
set.seed(123)
boot_means <- bootstrap_mean(n, B, sleep, 2)
p1 <- data.frame(means = boot_means) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = means)) +
  geom_histogram(col = "white", bins = 40) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean of average sleep (hours)", title = "Bootstrap distribution")  +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(text = element_text(size = 20))+
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 8) 
p1
```
:::
::::
::::::::

## Bootstrap to null distribution

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r fig.height=8}
p1 + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = xbar, col = "pink", size = 2) +
  labs(caption = expression(paste("pink line = ", bar(x)[obs]))) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 28))
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
-   This is **not** the null distribution! The null distribution should be centered at $\mu_{0} = `r mu0`$

-   However, the null distribution *should* have the same variability in $\bar{x}$ as the bootstrap distribution.
:::
:::::

-   So to get the null distribution, why not just **shift** the bootstrap distribution to be centered where we want it to be?

## Shifting the bootstrap distribution

-   In this example, bootstrap distribution is centered at $\bar{x}_{obs} = `r xbar`$

-   In order to center this distribution at $\mu_{0} = `r mu0`$, just subtract $`r xbar` - `r mu0` = `r xbar - mu0`$ from every single bootstrapped mean

    -   This will give us a simulated distribution for $\bar{x}$ centered at $\mu_{0} = `r mu0`$, which is exactly the null distribution!

    -   ::: {style="color: maroon"}
        We call this "shifting the bootstrap distribution", because we simply shift where the bootstrap distribution is centered
        :::

::: fragment
```{r echo = T}
mu0 <- 7.5

# xbar holds observed sample mean
shift <- xbar - mu0

# boot_means is a vector holding B bootstrapped sample means
null_dist <- boot_means - shift
```
:::

## Null distribution

```{r}
null_dist_df <- data.frame(means = null_dist) |>
  mutate(extreme = (means <= mu0 + shift  ))
p2 <-  null_dist_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = means)) +
  geom_histogram(col = "white", bins = 40) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean of average sleep (hours)", title = "Null distribution")  +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(text = element_text(size = 20))+
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 8) 
library(patchwork)
p1 + p2
```

-   ::: {style="color: maroon"}
    Notice where the distributions are centered. Also note: graphs aren't exactly identical due to binning of histogram.
    :::

## Obtain the p-value

$H_{0}$: $\mu =$ `r mu0` versus $H_{A}$: $\mu <$ `r mu0`

Our observed sample mean is $\bar{x}_{obs} =$ `r xbar`.

::::::: columns
:::: column
```{r}
p2
```

::: discuss
How do we find our p-value?
:::
::::

:::: column
::: fragment
```{r}
p2 +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = extreme), col = "white", bins = 40, alpha = 0.8)+ 
  geom_vline(xintercept = xbar, col = "magenta", size = 2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey30", "magenta")) +
  guides(fill = "none")
p_val <-mean(null_dist_df$extreme) 
```
:::

-   In `r B` iterations, simulated `r sum(null_dist_df$extreme)` "as more extreme" than our data, so p-value is approximately `r p_val`.
::::
:::::::

## Make decision and conclusion

::: discuss
Make a decision and conclusion in the context of the research question.
:::

-   Since our p-value of `r p_val` is less than the significance level of 0.05, we reject $H_{0}$. We have convincing evidence to suggest that the true mean of the average hours of sleep per night that a Middlebury student with an 8:15am course receives per night is less than 7.5 hours.

## Two-sided alternative hypothesis

What if instead, I am interested in learning if Middlebury students who have an 8:15am class get 7.5 hours of sleep or not (on average). Then our hypotheses are:

$$H_{0}: \mu = `r mu0` \qquad \text{ vs. } \qquad H_{A}: \mu \neq `r mu0`$$

::: discuss
-   What does it mean to be "as or more extreme" now? Remember, $\bar{x}_{obs} = `r xbar`$
:::

## Two-sided alternative hypothesis

We can be extreme in **both** the positive and negative direction of $\mu_{0}$!

::: fragment
```{r fig.height=4}
null_dist_df <- data.frame(means = null_dist) |>
  mutate(extreme = (means <= mu0 + shift ) | (means >= mu0 - shift))

null_dist_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = means, fill = extreme)) +
  geom_histogram(col = "white", bins = 40) +
  labs(title = "Null distribution", x = "Sample mean of average sleep (hours)")  +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(text = element_text(size = 20)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey30", "magenta")) +
  guides(fill = "none")+
  geom_vline(xintercept = xbar, col = "magenta", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu0 - shift,  col = "magenta", size = 2)
p_val <- mean(null_dist_df$extreme)

```
:::

-   Note that there are now `r sum(null_dist_df$extreme)` simulations that are "as or more extreme", so p-value is approximately `r p_val`.

## Obtain the p-value (cont.)

Let $shift$ represent the amount we shifted the bootstrap distribution by:

$$shift = `r xbar` - `r mu0` = `r xbar - mu0`$$

-   Simulated sample means as or more extreme as the following will contribute:

    -   $\mu_{0} + shift = `r mu0` + `r shift` = `r mu0+shift`$ , or

    -   $\mu_{0} - shift = `r mu0` - `r shift` = `r mu0 - shift`$

-   **Note that how you code will depend on if shift is positive or negative. That's why it's important to summarise your data in step 2!**

::: fragment
```{r echo = T}
sum( (null_dist <= mu0 + shift) | (null_dist >= mu0 - shift))/B
```
:::

## Make decision and conclusion

::: discuss
Make a decision and conclusion in the context of the research question.
:::

-   Since our p-value of `r p_val` is less than the significance level of 0.05, we reject $H_{0}$. We have convincing evidence to suggest that the true mean of the average hours of sleep per night that a Middlebury student with an 8:15am course receives per night is **different from** 7.5 hours.

## Comprehension questions

-   Why did we shift the bootstrap distribution?

-   Why can't we simulate null world like we did in the case of proportions?

-   How does the p-value from a two-sided $H_{A}$ compare to that of a one-sided $H_{A}$?

-   How is this different from the homework problem where you're comparing two means?
